## Welcome {#home}

### Other Significant NCDs

**Learning Objectives:**

- Distinguish coronary heart disease from rheumatic heart disease
- Describe COPD and chronic kidney disease as major NCD contributors
- Outline India's deafness and oral health programmes
- Recognize tobacco control as a cross-cutting NCD intervention

🟢 **MUST KNOW** · 🟡 **SHOULD KNOW** · 🟣 **MAY KNOW** · 🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.notes}
This closing module of the Selected NCDs series gathers several
NMC-listed conditions that share risk-factor overlap with diabetes,
hypertension, and stroke (already covered) without individually
needing a full module of their own.
:::

---

## Coronary Heart Disease vs. Rheumatic Heart Disease {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

Both affect the heart, but arise through entirely different mechanisms
— a frequently tested distinction:

| Feature | Coronary Heart Disease (CHD) | Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD) |
|---|---|---|
| **Mechanism** | Atherosclerotic narrowing of coronary arteries | Autoimmune damage to heart valves following **untreated streptococcal throat infection** (rheumatic fever) |
| **Risk factors** | Hypertension, diabetes, smoking, dyslipidaemia (shared with stroke, Module 3) | Overcrowding, poor access to antibiotic treatment for strep throat |
| **Population pattern** | Rising with urbanization and NCD risk-factor prevalence | Declining with improved living standards and antibiotic access, but still significant in lower-resource settings |

**Why RHD is particularly a "social" NCD:** unlike CHD's individual
risk-factor profile, RHD's root cause is a **treatable childhood
infection** — meaning its persistence reflects healthcare access
gaps as much as any biological risk factor.

---

## COPD and Chronic Kidney Disease {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

- **Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)** — progressive
  airflow limitation, strongly linked to **tobacco smoking** and, in
  India specifically, **indoor air pollution from solid-fuel cooking**
  (a direct link to Chapter 16's household air pollution content) —
  making COPD risk gendered, since women who cook are disproportionately
  exposed
- **Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)** — progressive, irreversible kidney
  function decline; **diabetes and hypertension are the leading
  causes** (recall Modules 1 and 2's complications content), making CKD
  less a standalone disease than a shared downstream consequence of
  the NCD risk factors already covered throughout this series

**Why grouping these together matters:** neither disease has a single
dominant cause the way, say, rheumatic heart disease does — both
emerge from the same overlapping web of tobacco, air pollution, and
metabolic risk factors running through this entire module series.

---

## Deafness and Oral Health {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

- **National Programme for Prevention and Control of Deafness (NPPCD)**
  — addresses hearing loss through early screening (including newborn
  hearing screening), treatment of correctable causes (chronic ear
  infection, wax impaction), and hearing aid provision
- **National Oral Health Programme (NOHP)** — addresses dental caries
  and periodontal disease, integrating oral health screening into
  general primary care rather than treating it as a separate
  specialty concern

**Shared pattern with the rest of this module:** both conditions are
common, often under-prioritized relative to their disease burden, and
addressed through **screening integrated into the general health
system** — the same primary-care integration principle already seen
throughout this curriculum (NLEP, DMHP, NPCBVI).

---

## Tobacco Control: A Cross-Cutting Intervention {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

Tobacco doesn't belong to just one disease in this module — it is a
shared risk factor for CHD, COPD, and multiple cancers (Module 4)
simultaneously, which is why India addresses it through its own
dedicated legal and programmatic framework:

- **National Tobacco Control Programme (NTCP)** — awareness, cessation
  services, and enforcement support
- **COTPA (Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act)** — India's core
  tobacco-control legislation: bans smoking in public places, prohibits
  tobacco advertising, mandates pictorial health warnings on packaging
- **WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC)** — the
  international treaty India is party to, providing the global
  policy architecture (taxation, advertising bans, packaging
  requirements) that COTPA implements domestically
- **Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Act (PECA), 2019** — a newer,
  separate law banning the production, sale, and advertisement of
  e-cigarettes/vapes in India — closing a gap COTPA (written before
  e-cigarettes existed) did not cover

**Why tobacco control is treated as its own topic, not folded into
any one disease:** a single successful tobacco-control policy
simultaneously reduces CHD, COPD, and cancer risk at once — a rare
example of one intervention addressing three separate disease burdens
in this curriculum simultaneously.

## Self-Check: Question 1 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 1

Rheumatic heart disease results from:

- Atherosclerotic narrowing of coronary arteries
- [Autoimmune damage to heart valves following untreated streptococcal throat infection]{.correct data-explanation="RHD arises from an autoimmune reaction to rheumatic fever, itself a consequence of untreated strep throat -- a fundamentally different mechanism from coronary heart disease's atherosclerotic process."}
- Chronic tobacco exposure
- Diabetic complications
:::

## Self-Check: Question 2 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 2

In India specifically, which additional exposure (beyond tobacco
smoking) raises COPD risk, especially among women?

- Excess dietary salt
- [Indoor air pollution from solid-fuel cooking]{.correct data-explanation="Household air pollution from solid-fuel cooking is a major COPD risk factor in India, disproportionately affecting women who do most of the cooking -- connecting directly to the household air pollution content in the Environment section."}
- High-altitude living
- Excess physical activity
:::

## Self-Check: Question 3 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 3

The two leading causes of chronic kidney disease are:

- Tobacco use and alcohol
- [Diabetes and hypertension]{.correct data-explanation="Diabetes and hypertension are the leading causes of CKD, making it less a standalone disease than a downstream consequence of the same metabolic risk factors covered in the diabetes and hypertension modules."}
- Rheumatic fever and COPD
- Cancer and cataract
:::
